newsitem.title: USA: Goldman did not deceive municipalities - spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Goldman did not deceive municipalities - spokesman.

text.p: A spokesmen for one of the top two underwriters of negotiated advance refundings between 1990 and 1995 said the firm did not deceive municipalities by secretly inflating prices on the U.S. Treasuries they sold.

Goldman Sachs & Co was responding to charges by the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority on Tuesday that localities were "exploited and deceived" by Wall Street firms that "knowingly" inflated prices on escrow securities above fair market value.
Goldman Sachs spokesman Peter Rose told Reuters, "We believe that any actions the firm took on behalf of issuers are proper and legal."
A spokesman for Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, which is ranked as the other top underwriter of the deals, had no comment.

The $1.3 trillion municipal bond market has been rocked by allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond financing transactions, a practice dubbed "yield burning."

The L.A. county authority made the charges in a 43-page comment letter to the Internal Revenue Service, which in July said localities that paid more than fair market value for Treasuries can enter into "closing agreements" with the IRS to avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable.
Goldman's Rose said firm officials had not yet seen the county authority's letter and, therefore, had no further comment.
PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, meanwhile, urged the IRS in a 15-page comment letter to revoke the closing agreement program.

Under the IRS' controversial closing agreement plan, issuers can avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable by paying the Treasury the difference between the price the issuer paid and the spot price of the securities on the date of purchase, plus interest. PSA said a closing agreement program that relies on spot price or any other "rigid approach to market valuation" is deeply flawed.
The group urged IRS to continue its practice of determining fair market value on a case-by-case basis.
PSA added that muni bond issuers are not as unsophisticated as the IRS seems to think.

"Issuers do not universally lack" as the IRS procedure "seems to imply, either the sophistication or adequate incentives to obtain the best prices from their counter parties," the bond dealer group said.
